title: Backyard Putting Greens in Fort Collins, CO | NoCo Turf Co.
description: A backyard green on an existing Fort Collins lot sits outside the city's turf ban; a green in a new development's plan does not. Plus the city courses' greens.
h1: In Fort Collins, a putting green behind an existing house is exempt; one in a new development's landscape plan is not.

display.paint: behind an existing house is exempt

lede: Fort Collins' development turf ban has one exception, an athletic field of play, and a putting green isn't it. The ban never reaches the backyard of a home that's already built, though, and the city's three golf courses keep practice greens anyone can roll before choosing a speed.

answer.question: Can I put an artificial putting green in my Fort Collins backyard?
answer.answer: Yes, if the house already stands on a single- or two-unit lot. Fort Collins' Land Use Code 5.10.1 exempts development on those existing lots from its artificial-turf ban. Inside a new development's landscape plan the ban applies, and its only exception is an athletic field of play, which a putting green is not. Not legal advice.

blocks.h2: The city's one turf exception is an athletic field, and a green isn't one.
blocks.takeaway: A green added to an existing house lot is outside the section; a green drawn into a new development's landscape plan has no way in.
paras: Section 5.10.1 governs the landscape plans that development in Fort Collins has to file, and it carves out development on existing house lots with one or two units and accessory dwellings. A green built behind a finished house falls in that gap, so the city's turf ban isn't the question for it. The [Fort Collins turf page](/areas/fort-collins-co/) covers that clause in full.

Inside a development landscape plan the answer flips. The Director may allow artificial turf only on an athletic field of play, and only after deciding the use is appropriate, adds no pollutants that could cause environmental impairment and has no reasonable alternative. Colorado's 2025 amendment counts chipping and putting greens as functional turf, but the Fort Collins exception doesn't name them, so a clubhouse practice green, an apartment amenity green or a model-home green in a new plan falls outside it.

The same section lets a new development plant high-water live turf on the playing areas of golf courses. For a lot in a subdivision still being built out, whether a green belongs to the development's plan or comes after the house is finished depends on the permit record: ask Fort Collins Planning before breaking ground. Not legal advice.

blocks.h2: Collindale, Southridge and City Park Nine all keep practice greens you can roll before settling on a speed.
paras: The City of Fort Collins runs three golf courses. Collindale, 18 holes on 160 acres in southeast Fort Collins, is recognized, the city says, for some of the fastest greens in the state, hosts local U.S. Open qualifying, and has an oversized putting green plus a practice green with a greenside bunker. Southridge, also in southeast Fort Collins, plays 18 holes on 128 acres and has a chipping green and a putting green beside its range. City Park Nine, the 9-hole course built in 1940 beside City Park, pairs small greens and tight fairways with a bunkered chipping green and two practice putting greens.

Those practice greens are the closest public reference in town for the speed and break of a backyard green. Roll a few putts on Collindale's oversized green and a few on City Park Nine's, and you have two real surfaces to point to when you describe what you want at home.

blocks.h2: The Fort Collins Country Club sits on county land, so a lot nearby may not be the city's to rule on.
paras: Larimer County's parcel records mark both parcels of the private Fort Collins Country Club on Country Club Road as unincorporated, outside the city. A home near the club can carry a Fort Collins mailing address and still fall under Larimer County land-use rules instead of the city's Land Use Code.

Look up the parcel before planning a green there. If Larimer County's parcel map shows the lot as unincorporated, section 5.10.1 does not govern it; the county's own land-use code does, and its planning staff can say whether it has anything to add for a backyard green on that lot.

faq.q: Can a putting green run into the strip between my sidewalk and the street in Fort Collins?
faq.a: No. That parkway strip is city right-of-way, and the Streetscape Standards the city adopted in December 2025 say no artificial turf may be included in any streetscape. Keep the green and its fringe on your side of the sidewalk.

faq.q: Can the green go in a Fort Collins front yard?
faq.a: On an existing single- or two-unit lot, the Land Use Code's turf section doesn't reach the front yard either; the city-owned parkway past the sidewalk is the exception. An HOA's design rules can still govern how a front-yard green looks.

faq.q: Will Fort Collins Utilities' Xeriscape Incentive Program pay toward a green?
faq.a: Unlikely. The program pays to replace grass with an eligible low-water landscape, its page doesn't list artificial turf as one, and the city says XIP rebates are funded by a grant from the state, while Colorado bars state turf-replacement grant money from paying for artificial turf. Plan a green as its own project, separate from any XIP renovation.
